canonicalExplanation.summary: Selectors **find** existing elements in the DOM so rules can style them — they never create or move HTML. Core kinds: **type** (`h2`), **class** (`.card__title`), **attribute** (`[type="email"]`, `a[href^="https"]`), and **combinators** that describe relationships: descendant (space), child (`>`), next sibling (`+`), later sibling (`~`). Good selectors target an element's **role** directly, not a fragile chain of wrappers.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
A card title is styled with `main div.content > div div:nth-child(2) h2`. A designer adds one wrapper div — and every title loses its style. The selector was tied to the page's scaffolding, not to what the element *is*. A .card__title class targets the component role without depending on three wrapper levels. In this lesson you'll choose selectors that are specific enough without coupling to incidental nesting.

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.body: You should know **Specificity and source order**, **Text and page semantics**, **Rules, declarations and values**, and **Document tree and DOM concept** — selectors match nodes in the DOM tree.

sections.heading: The model: match by role, relationship when it matters
sections.body:
| Selector | Matches |
|---|---|
| `h2`. | every h2. |
| `.card__title`. | elements with that class. |
| `[type="email"]`. | elements with that attribute value. |
| `a[href^="https"]`. | links whose href starts with https. |
| `.card p`. | p anywhere inside .card (descendant). |
| `.menu > li`. | li that are direct children of .menu. |
| `h2 + p`. | the p right after an h2. |
| `h2 ~ p`. | every later sibling p of an h2. |

```css
.card__title { font-size: 1.25rem; }      /* role-based, robust */
.menu > li { display: inline-block; }     /* relationship matters here */
```

```reveal
{"prompt": "When is a combinator the right choice?", "answer": "When the relationship is part of the meaning — e.g. only direct menu items, or the paragraph right after a heading. Not just to reach an element buried in wrappers."}
```

sections.heading: Fragile vs robust

includes: Use type, class, attribute and combinator selectors.
Prefer role-based classes over long chains tied to incidental nesting.

outcomes: Choose selectors that are specific enough without coupling to incidental nesting.

examples.title: Targeting a card title directly
examples.situation: A .card__title class targets the component role without depending on three wrapper levels.
walkthrough: **Before:** `main div.content > div div:nth-child(2) h2` depended on three wrapper levels and scored (0,2,5).
**After:** add `class="card__title"` to the h2 and select `.card__title` — (0,1,0), matching by component role.
**Test:** add a wrapper div and move the card; the browser will still render the title correctly.
examples.result: The title style survives layout changes because the selector targets what the element is.

examples.title: Styling external links
examples.situation: The site wants a small arrow after links that go to other websites.
walkthrough: An attribute selector can match without extra classes: `a[href^="http"]`.
Internal links use relative hrefs, so they don't match.
Refine: `a[href^="http"]:not([href*="codestead.example"])` to exclude absolute links to your own site.
examples.result: External links are marked automatically, based on their real attribute values.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: A selector describes how the browser should create or rearrange HTML elements.
misconceptions.correction: Selectors only match elements that already exist in the DOM; they can't create, remove or reorder elements. Choose selectors that identify an element's role rather than its incidental position.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In the opening predict, what can selectors actually do?

analogy.example: Selectors are like **search filters in a contacts app**: "people tagged 'family'" (class), "people in Mumbai" (attribute), "children of Asha" (combinator). Filters find contacts — they never create new ones.
usefulFor: tag by role for robust searches
limitations: "Third person on page two" is a fragile filter — like nth-child chains.

steps.explanation: The old selector depends on incidental nesting.
A .card__title class names the component role in the HTML.
The class targets the component role without depending on three wrapper levels.

nearTransfer.prompt: Write selectors for: (a) all required inputs, (b) list items directly inside `.steps`, (c) the first paragraph right after any h2.

farTransfer.prompt: Find the three longest selectors in a stylesheet you know. Refactor each into a role-based class or a meaningful relationship, and prove the page looks the same.
scaffold: Add classes in HTML where needed.

remediation.explanation: For each selector ask: **Does it describe what this element is, or where it happens to sit?** If it's the second, add a meaningful class — unless the relationship itself matters.

recap.summary: To choose selectors that are specific enough without coupling to incidental nesting, match elements by role with classes or attributes, use combinators only when the relationship matters, and remember selectors only find existing elements.
